newsitem.title: USA: Green groups fear weakening of U.S. fisheries bill.
newsitem.headline: Green groups fear weakening of U.S. fisheries bill.

text.p: With time running out to wrap up action this session, senators on Friday were fine-tuning a bill to transform a law encouraging exploitation of U.S. fisheries into a law to conserve declining resources.

Environmental and wildlife groups said they feared delays would result in a weaker bill but said that would be better than sticking with current law that has seen a drastic decline of U.S. marine life and many fishing communities.

"It is such a dramatic bill that even if they weasel it it's still significantly better than today," said Gerry Leape of Greenpeace. Critics such as Greenpeace have said for the last 20 years the Magnuson Fisheries Act, enacted to keep foreign vessels from exploiting U.S. waters, has given U.S. fishermen free rein to overfish.
Backers of the bill still hoped for a full Senate vote next week on the measure to overhaul the Magnuson Act but admitted a vote might slip to the following week.

Conservation and environmental groups prefer the version the House of Representatives passed last year and worry there will not be time to meld House measures into the Senate bill. They fear the House simply will have to accept the Senate version in order to get a bill passed at all.

"It is a little frustrating for us. We passed our bill almost a year ago, now they're sending something back that reflects very little of what was in the House bill," said an aide to the House Resources Committee, which shepherded that body's bill. "It may may be our members will accept it, but they may not."

Both House and Senate bills clamp down on overfishing and the amount of bycatch, commercially undesirable marine life that is dumped dead or dying back into the ocean. They also have provisions to restore degraded fish habitat including wetlands, estuaries and other coastal waterways that are crucial for marine life, and to help fishing communities, many of which have seen their fortunes fall along with dwindling fish populations.

Environmental groups said the House language on conservation rules was stronger, with fewer loopholes. The House bill also eliminated fishing rights that can be transferred and in the past generally have been accumulated by the larger fishing enterprises.

The Senate bill imposes a four-year moratorium on the transferable fishing quotas, shortening the moratorium by a year after senators from Washington state, home to most of the big factory fishing trawlers, said they would try to kill the bill unless there were compromises on the fishing quotas.

Washington Sens. Slade Gorton, a Republican, and Patty Murray, a Democrat, raised other objections to the bill, which prompted its sponsor, Alaska Republican Ted Stevens, to say the main issue was factory trawlers' objections to curbing wasteful fishing practices.
